incidents.title: Gift cards double-spent in a split
incidents.brief: The US-EU link drops for 90 s. EU checkout keeps approving gift-card spends from a stale local balance while US users spend the same cards.
incidents.constraint: Balances must never go negative; reviews and carts can tolerate divergence.
incidents.question: Now what partition policy stops double spends in the next split?

users: gift-card redeem approved in EU while link down
us: replication link to EU: DOWN for 90 s
gift card gc_3391 balance 0 after $50 debit at 12:04:11
eu: replica lag: unknown, last sync 90 s ago
local read gc_3391 balance $50, approved debit $50 at 12:04:13
no quorum check on debit path

choices.label: Require a quorum-confirmed debit, reject spends when unreachable
choices.resultBody: EU spends fail fast during the 90 s split instead of approving money the US side may already have spent; carts and reviews stay writable.

choices.label: Accept spends locally and merge balances by latest timestamp
choices.resultBody: Last-write-wins keeps only one region's balance, so two $50 spends against a $50 card both succeed and one debit is silently lost.

choices.label: Accept spends locally and retry the US primary until it acks
choices.resultBody: The shopper already got an approval, so background retries are reconciliation after the fact; the double spend has happened.

hints: Which data is cheap to reconcile and which is money?
An approval is a promise the other region never saw.
Pick consistency for balances, availability for the rest.

mitigation.question: The link is still down and double spends keep landing. What stops the bleeding now?

choices.label: Flag off EU gift-card redemption until the link heals
choices.resultBody: EU shoppers see "gift cards unavailable, try again shortly" while carts and card payments keep flowing. No new double spends land, but the next split needs the same manual flag.

choices.label: Add two EU replica nodes so approvals clear faster
choices.resultBody: The two new EU nodes copy the same stale balances, so they approve already-spent cards faster; double spends keep landing.

choices.label: Restart EU checkout pods to drop their cached balances
choices.resultBody: Fresh pods read balances from the EU replica, which is still cut off from the US, so within a minute they approve the same spent cards again.

incidents.title: Every feature went read-only
incidents.brief: During a 2-minute partition the EU site rejected likes, carts and logins because the whole database was configured CP.
incidents.constraint: Only payments need strong consistency; the rest merges cleanly.
incidents.question: How should the team change the partition policy?

choices.label: CP for payments only; AP with merge rules for the rest
choices.resultTitle: EU stays useful in a split
choices.resultBody: Likes, carts and sessions accept local writes and merge on heal, while only payment writes wait for a quorum; errors drop to near zero.

choices.label: Raise the cross-region write timeout from 2 s to 30 s
choices.resultBody: A partition does not heal faster because clients wait longer; users now stare at spinners for 30 s before the same error.

choices.label: Route every EU request to the US region during splits
choices.resultTitle: The US is exactly what EU cannot reach
choices.resultBody: During a partition the EU clients cannot reach the US region either, so rerouting adds latency and still ends in errors.

hints: Is every feature equally dangerous to diverge?
CAP is a per-operation choice.
Keep strictness where divergence costs money.

incidents.title: Like counts drop after heal
incidents.brief: Likes now merge after a split. After last night's 2-minute split, 12,400 likes vanished: each region's counter was merged by keeping the newer total.
incidents.constraint: Likes must stay writable in a split; payments stay CP.
incidents.question: What merge rule keeps both regions' likes?

choices.label: Store per-region counts and sum them on merge (PN-counter)
choices.resultBody: Each region increments only its own slot, and a merge keeps the max of each slot and sums them, so both sides' likes survive any split. Cost: one slot per region per counter.

choices.label: Resync every like count from the US primary after each heal
choices.resultBody: Copying the US total over EU throws away every like EU accepted during the split; the loss is now just predictable.

choices.label: Move likes to CP with payments so they never diverge
choices.resultBody: During the next split EU users can't like anything, recreating the outage the per-feature change just fixed.

hints: What does 'keep the newer total' throw away?
Each region counted its own likes independently.
Give each region its own slot and combine the slots.

incidents.title: Feed reads pay the ocean tax
incidents.brief: No partition today, yet every feed read in Singapore goes to the US leader: 180 ms extra per request.
incidents.constraint: Feeds may be a few seconds stale; profile edits must show to the author.
incidents.question: What does PACELC suggest for normal operation?

choices.label: Serve feed reads from the local follower, author reads from leader
choices.resultBody: The Else branch of PACELC trades a little staleness for latency on feeds, while read-your-writes routing keeps the author's own edits visible.

choices.label: Make SG replication synchronous so local reads are always fresh
choices.resultTitle: Writes now wait on the ocean
choices.resultBody: Every write must cross the Pacific before acking, so write latency jumps by the round trip and a slow link stalls the leader.

choices.label: Move the US leader to a larger instance with faster disks
choices.resultBody: The 180 ms is network round trip, not server time; a bigger leader shaves a few milliseconds off a delay caused by geography.

hints: There's no partition. What's the tradeoff now?
Latency or consistency, every read.
Who actually needs the freshest copy?

variants.constraint: Feeds carry legal takedowns that must vanish in Singapore the moment they commit. Writes are 0.5% of traffic, and a 180 ms slower write is acceptable.

sync-all.resultBody: The leader waits for Singapore's ack before committing, so a takedown reaches the local replica before anyone can read it; feed reads stay local at about 150 ms p95. Cost: writes pay the 180 ms round trip, and a Singapore outage stalls them.

local-follower.resultBody: Reads are fast, but async replication leaves the Singapore follower 1-3 s behind, so a taken-down post stays visible to local readers after it commits, which the legal rule forbids.

hints: There's no partition, but the freshness rule has changed.
Writes are rare; reads are 200 times more common.
Pay the ocean round trip on the operation that happens least often.

incidents.title: APAC feeds run a minute behind
incidents.brief: Feed reads now hit the SG follower. A US backfill pushed its replay lag to 45 s, so APAC feeds show 45-second-old comments and support tickets pile up.
incidents.constraint: Feeds may be a few seconds stale, not a minute; the backfill must finish tonight.
incidents.question: How do you keep feeds within their staleness budget?

choices.label: Read from the leader when follower lag exceeds 5 s

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Bounded staleness: reads pay the ocean round trip only while the follower is behind.

choices.resultBody: The router checks the follower's replay lag; while the backfill runs, feed reads go to the US leader at +180 ms, then return to SG once it catches up.

choices.label: Add a second SG follower and split the feed reads across both
choices.resultBody: Both followers replay the same backfill stream from the leader, so each is 45 s behind; the reads are split, the staleness is not.

choices.label: Cache feed pages in SG for 60 s to hide the churn
choices.resultBody: A 60 s cache stacked on a 45 s replay lag serves feeds up to 105 s old; comments still vanish, and now for longer.

hints: Is the follower slow, or just behind?
Staleness is a number the router can read.
Bound how stale a follower read may be.

incidents.title: Inventory oversold after heal
incidents.brief: Both regions sold the last 40 concert seats during a 3-minute split. After heal, 38 seats were sold twice.
incidents.constraint: Seats are unique; overselling means refunds and angry fans.
incidents.question: Which design prevents double-sold seats during a partition?

choices.label: Give each seat block one owning region; others must reach it
choices.resultBody: A seat is only sold by its owner region, so a partitioned region refuses that block instead of selling it twice; the other blocks keep selling.

choices.label: Let both regions sell and resolve conflicts with a CRDT counter
choices.resultBody: A CRDT can merge a count, but it cannot un-sell seat 14B to the second buyer; uniqueness needs a single decision point.

choices.label: Order conflicting sales by synchronized wall-clock timestamps
choices.resultBody: Picking a winner after heal still means one fan was charged and emailed a ticket that no longer exists; the refund storm is the incident.

hints: Can two regions both own the same seat?
Merging after the fact still means a broken promise.
Give each item a single place to decide.

users: block A12-A52: 40 seats left when the link dropped at 14:21:03
after heal: 38 seats sold in both US and EU, 38 refunds queued
us: link to EU down 14:21:03 to 14:24:05, local writes still accepted
sold 38 of the last 40 seats with no cross-region check
CPU 81%, no errors returned to buyers
eu: link to US down 14:21:03 to 14:24:05, local writes still accepted
sold the same 38 seats locally, no cross-region check
CPU 78%, no errors returned to buyers

incidents.title: Quorum reads timing out
incidents.brief: The team set every read to QUORUM across three regions. p95 read latency hit 900 ms and the product page is timing out.
incidents.constraint: Product descriptions change a few times a day; stock counts need care.
incidents.question: How should read consistency be tuned?

choices.label: Use ONE for descriptions, LOCAL_QUORUM for stock reads
choices.resultBody: Descriptions read from the nearest replica in single-digit milliseconds, and stock checks use a local-region quorum instead of waiting on every ocean.

choices.label: Keep cross-region QUORUM and add a 24-hour cache for stock
choices.resultTitle: Stale stock for a whole day
choices.resultBody: The cache hides the latency but serves stock counts up to a day old, so the page shows items that sold out this morning.

choices.label: Drop every read, including stock, to consistency level ONE
choices.resultBody: Descriptions got fast, but stock checks can now read a lagging replica and show sold-out items as available.

hints: Does every field need the same guarantee?
Nearest-replica reads are cheap; ocean quorums are not.
Tune consistency per query, not per cluster.

variants.constraint: Stock now shows only as an 'in stock' badge, and checkout re-verifies every item with the reservation service before charging. Replica CPU is the budget to protect.

all-one.resultBody: Every page read, badge included, hits one nearby replica, so p95 drops to about 290 ms and replica work shrinks. A stale badge is harmless because checkout re-verifies stock. Cost: a sold-out item can show 'in stock' for a second or two.

tune-per-query.resultBody: It works, but each LOCAL_QUORUM stock read touches two replicas to protect a badge nobody relies on, since checkout re-verifies anyway; replica CPU sits at 44% instead of 38%, and badge reads stall when a local replica is slow.

hints: Ask which reads on this page still need any guarantee at all.
Checkout checks stock again with its own service before charging.
If a stale answer is caught downstream, how many replicas must agree on this read?

incidents.title: Shopping carts lose items
incidents.brief: After a 60 s split, shoppers find items missing from their carts. Conflicting carts were resolved by keeping the newest copy.
incidents.constraint: Carts should never silently lose an add.
incidents.question: What merge rule fits the cart?

choices.label: Merge conflicting carts as a union of adds, reconcile removes
choices.resultBody: Both regions' adds survive the heal; a rare resurrected item is cheap to fix at checkout, unlike a sale lost to a vanished item.

choices.label: Reject cart writes whenever the other region is unreachable
choices.resultTitle: Carts went dark for a minute
choices.resultBody: Shoppers can't add anything for the whole 60 s split, so sales are lost to protect data that merges almost for free.

choices.label: Keep the newest cart but sync clocks with a tighter NTP interval
choices.resultBody: Better clocks pick the winner more accurately, but last-write-wins still discards every add made on the losing side.

hints: What does keeping the newest copy throw away?
Adds from two sides can be combined.
Choose a merge that never loses an add.

users: 220 tickets: 'item missing from my cart' after 10:03
every affected cart was edited from two regions during the split
us: partition 10:02:11 to 10:03:11, both sides kept accepting cart writes
merge of cart c-8812: us version [A, B] at 10:02:40, eu version [A, C] at 10:02:52
resolution: newest timestamp wins, kept eu version, B discarded
eu: cart c-8812: add C accepted at 10:02:52
heal: eu copy newer by 12 s, overwrote the us copy
no record that the us copy held an item the eu copy lacked

incidents.title: Payments reject writes as if partitioned
incidents.brief: CoinPurse's CP payments store runs 3 replicas in one region. Every few minutes writes are rejected for about 12 s, as if the network had split.
incidents.constraint: The network is healthy, the leak fix ships Monday, and a fresh process takes two days to fill its heap again.
incidents.question: What stops the write rejections before Monday?

choices.label: Hand off leadership, then restart the leaking replica

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: One planned leader handoff and a restart; it treats the symptom until Monday's fix and keeps payments CP.

choices.resultBody: A planned leadership transfer to replica A costs one sub-second blip instead of a 12 s election. Replica C restarts with an empty heap, the GC pauses stop, and rejected writes drop to zero. Nothing about the consistency model had to change.

choices.label: Switch payment writes to AP and merge balances on heal
choices.resultBody: Writes stop failing, but there was never a partition to survive. Now any replica accepts debits on its own, and within a day two concurrent spends against the same wallet both succeed and one is lost on merge.

choices.label: Raise the election timeout from 5 s to 30 s to ride out pauses
choices.resultBody: Pauses no longer trigger elections, so rejected writes drop to 1% and p99 eases to 6 s. Leader C's pauses have grown from 9 s to 11 s since yesterday.

hints: Check whether the network actually split, or a node just stopped answering.
Losing availability does not always mean you need a different consistency model.
The fix for the leak is already written. What resets a full heap tonight?

a: 14:02:11 no heartbeat from leader C for 5.0 s
14:02:23 lost election: C has the longer log, term 44
b: 14:02:12 granted vote to A for term 43
14:02:23 granted vote to C for term 44
c: 14:02:11 stepping down: saw term 43 from A

culprit.explanation: Replica C's own log shows 9 s GC pauses with an old generation still 97% full after collection: the leaking leader freezes, misses heartbeats, and each pause costs a 12 s election.

wrongNodeFeedback.users: The API only reports the rejections; it retries correctly once a leader is back.
wrongNodeFeedback.a: A starts elections because it stopped hearing from C. That is a symptom, not the cause.
wrongNodeFeedback.b: B is healthy: low heap, fast disk. It just votes.

incidents.title: Payments freeze 40 s at a time
incidents.brief: The 30 s election timeout rode out C's pauses for a day, but the leak kept growing: pauses now pass 31 s, elections fire anyway, and each one freezes payments for 40 s.
incidents.constraint: The leak fix still ships Monday; the network is healthy.
incidents.question: What stops the 40-second freezes tonight?

choices.label: Hand leadership to A, restart C, reset timeout to 5 s
choices.resultBody: A planned transfer costs a sub-second blip, C restarts with an empty heap so the pauses stop, and the 5 s timeout means a real crash fails over quickly again.

choices.label: Raise the election timeout again, from 30 s to 60 s
choices.resultBody: The 31 s pauses stay under 60 s, so no elections fire, but every pause is 31 s without commits, and a real crash now takes a minute to fail over.

choices.label: Add a fourth replica so the pauses on leader C matter less
choices.resultBody: A fourth member does nothing for a leader that freezes: writes still stop for every pause, and four members tolerate no more failures than three.

hints: The pauses kept growing while the timeout hid them.
A longer timeout only changes how long a pause may freeze writes.
What resets a full heap without a 30 s election?

incidents.title: Cross-DC read repair spikes normal query latency
incidents.brief: With no network partition active, background read-repair across transatlantic regions pushes p95 latency to 340ms on simple catalog lookups.
incidents.constraint: Catalog data is updated once daily; read latency must remain under 60ms globally during steady state.
incidents.question: Under the PACELC theorem, what trade-off restores normal catalog read speed?

choices.label: Serve catalog reads from local quorum and defer repair to off-peak
choices.resultTitle: PACELC latency trade-off restored catalog speed
choices.resultBody: Under normal state (Else in PACELC), prioritizing Latency over Consistency avoids transatlantic blocking on read-repair.

choices.label: Force synchronous cross-region repair on all catalog read queries
choices.resultBody: Synchronous cross-region coordination forces every read to wait on transatlantic round-trips for non-critical catalog data.

choices.label: Implement two-phase locking across both datacenters on every query
choices.resultTitle: Distributed locks created massive read contention
choices.resultBody: Acquiring distributed locks across WAN links for pure read queries introduces extreme lock contention and head-of-line blocking.

hints: PACELC states that when there is no partition (E), choose Latency or Consistency.
Catalog updates happen once per day, making immediate cross-region consensus wasteful.
Local quorum avoids cross-continental round trips during standard queries.

incidents.title: WAN jitter triggers dual-primary split-brain writes
incidents.brief: Intermittent WAN packet loss causes the backup cluster in us-west to declare the us-east primary dead, accepting writes concurrently.
incidents.constraint: Financial account ledger balances must never accept split diverging transactions.
incidents.question: How should partition handling be hardened to guarantee consistency over availability?

choices.label: Enforce third-party arbiter quorum lease before any leader promotion
choices.resultBody: By requiring an independent third witness region for leader leases, isolated regions cannot unilaterally claim leadership.

choices.label: Shorten heartbeat timeout to promote the backup cluster even faster
choices.resultBody: Aggressive timeouts promoted the secondary on transient network hiccups, escalating the frequency of split-brain collisions.

choices.label: Allow writes on both clusters and merge conflicts later with timestamp
choices.resultTitle: Ledger balances silently corrupted by timestamp merge
choices.resultBody: Last-write-wins overwrote concurrent debits, violating the strict non-divergence financial ledger constraint.

hints: Two regions cannot safely decide a majority during a complete network severance.
An odd-numbered voter or third-party arbiter prevents symmetric claims to leadership.
In CP systems, refusing writes on the minority side is essential to preserve safety.

incidents.title: Live stream viewer counts stale during chat storm
incidents.brief: Real-time viewer counters lag behind by 45 seconds during viral celebrity streaming because counter updates require strict quorum serialization.
incidents.constraint: Viewer counts can tolerate rough approximations (+-5%), but streaming chat must remain responsive.
incidents.question: How should the counter architecture be relaxed to satisfy PACELC AP expectations?

choices.label: Switch to local PN-counter CRDTs with periodic asynchronous gossip
choices.resultTitle: CRDT counters absorbed massive concurrent increments
choices.resultBody: Conflict-free replicated data types allow local non-blocking increments, converging accurately without quorum locks.

choices.label: Route all viewer increments through a single distributed Redis lock
choices.resultTitle: Lock serialization bottlenecked the counter pipeline
choices.resultBody: Serializing 90,000 updates per second through a single lock created a catastrophic queue buildup.

choices.label: Write increments to every node synchronously to eliminate stale reads
choices.resultTitle: All-node synchronous writes magnified system latency
choices.resultBody: Writing synchronously to all replicas means latency is bound by the slowest node, crashing overall throughput.

hints: Counters do not need linearizable ordering if operations are commutative.
CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types) provide eventual consistency with zero write locking.
Trading strict consistency for low latency is the definition of the PA/EL branch in PACELC.

incidents.title: Hinted handoff storm saturates disk on surviving nodes
incidents.brief: During a 3-hour network partition, surviving nodes accepted writes on behalf of isolated peers, accumulating 400GB of hinted handoffs that threaten disk exhaustion.
incidents.constraint: Do not drop confirmed user transactions, but prevent coordinator nodes from running out of disk.
incidents.question: How should the hinted handoff accumulation be controlled during prolonged partitions?

choices.label: Cap hint storage window and fail fast to consistency errors once full
choices.resultTitle: Hint storage bounding protected coordinator survival
choices.resultBody: Limiting hint retention to 1 hour preserves disk safety; subsequent writes fail cleanly instead of crashing coordinators.

choices.label: Disable disk limits and keep spooling hints indefinitely in RAM buffer
choices.resultTitle: Coordinator nodes crashed with Out-Of-Memory errors
choices.resultBody: Spooling unbounded hints into memory exhausted JVM heaps, taking down surviving nodes that were serving traffic.

choices.label: Silently discard hints without returning any write error to callers
choices.resultTitle: Silent data loss corrupted customer order histories
choices.resultBody: Dropping hints without alerting callers acknowledged writes that never persisted, corrupting downstream records.

hints: Hinted handoff is an availability mechanism (AP) intended for brief transient disconnects.
Prolonged partitions turn hint queues into disk-filling liabilities.
Failing fast when hint thresholds are breached preserves node stability.

variants.constraint: Every write is acknowledged by a quorum of 3 replicas before any hint is stored, and a full anti-entropy repair runs as soon as a partition heals.

cap-10-silent-drop.resultBody: Once the hint window fills, coordinators stop storing hints but keep acking writes that already reached 2 of 3 replicas; disk stops growing, and repair rebuilds the isolated peer after heal. Cost: that replica lags until repair, so reads must use QUORUM.

cap-10-cap-hints.resultBody: After the 1-hour hint store fills, coordinators return consistency errors for writes that already reached 2 of 3 replicas. For the partition's last 2 hours durable writes fail, and client retries push errors to 900.

hints: Check how many replicas already hold each write before any hint exists.
A hint only speeds up catching one replica back up; something else repairs it anyway.
Writes that already met their consistency level needn't fail when the catch-up buffer does.

incidents.title: Cross-region session checkout reads stale inventory reservation
incidents.brief: Shoppers completing checkout in Asia see items disappear mid-payment because inventory read consistency level was set to ONE across global nodes.
incidents.constraint: Checkout inventory reservations must be monotonic without double-booking items.
incidents.question: Which quorum tuning guarantees strong read-your-own-writes across global regions?

choices.label: Enforce LOCAL_QUORUM reads and writes with session consistency tokens
choices.resultTitle: Session token guarantees causal inventory reads
choices.resultBody: Passing session tokens ensures subsequent reads reflect the caller's own reservation writes without global roundtrips.

choices.label: Switch all read and write queries globally to synchronous ALL quorum
choices.resultTitle: Global ALL quorum crushed throughput and availability
choices.resultBody: Requiring confirmation from every node globally caused requests to fail whenever any single remote region experienced jitter.

choices.label: Add artificial client sleep delays before calling checkout confirmation
choices.resultTitle: Sleep delays degraded checkout UX without safety
choices.resultBody: Arbitrary sleeps failed during replication lag spikes and unnecessarily penalised fast network connections.

hints: Session consistency guarantees that a client always reads their own previous writes.
LOCAL_QUORUM satisfies R + W > N locally without incurring inter-region latency.
Global ALL sacrifices availability whenever a single remote node degrades.

incidents.title: Wallet balances show old values after payments
incidents.brief: Since the 16:20 deploy, 6.2% of balance reads return the value from before the last payment and support gets 140 tickets/h. Read p99 improved to 8 ms and every node is up.
incidents.constraint: Payments are written at QUORUM; revert only the PR that broke reads.
incidents.question: Which PR do you revert?

choices.label: Revert PR #4410: compaction strategy from SizeTiered to Leveled
choices.resultBody: Leveled compaction changes disk layout and read amplification, not which replicas answer a read. Stale balances continue at about 6% and you have triggered another heavy compaction cycle.

choices.label: Revert PR #4416: hinted handoff window from 3 h to 6 h
choices.resultBody: A longer hint window only changes how long a down node collects missed writes. Reads are still served by one replica that may not have the latest write, so stale balances stay near 6%.

nodes.sub: hints kept longer, reads still stale

choices.label: Revert PR #4423: balance reads from LOCAL_QUORUM to LOCAL_ONE
choices.diff:
ledger-service/db/session.yaml
   keyspace: ledger
   table: balances
-  read_consistency: LOCAL_QUORUM
+  read_consistency: LOCAL_ONE
   write_consistency: LOCAL_QUORUM

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Slightly higher read latency for read-your-writes.

choices.resultBody: With reads at ONE, any single replica answers, and a replica that missed the write returns the old balance. LOCAL_QUORUM reads overlap the QUORUM writes (2 + 2 > 3), so they always include one up-to-date replica. Cost: p99 rises from 8 ms to 14 ms.

hints: The metric that improved is the clue: 8 ms means fewer replicas were asked.
Writes use QUORUM; check whether reads overlap them.
One diff lowers how many replicas must agree on a read.

incidents.title: The Cassandra bill is 40% of infra
incidents.brief: A three-datacenter Cassandra ring is healthy: 9 ms serving p99, 99.99% availability. The analytics DC of 12 nodes sits at 9% CPU because nightly Spark jobs run for only 2 hours. Finance wants savings.
incidents.constraint: SLOs: serving read p99 under 50 ms and availability above 99.95% with a node down.
incidents.question: What do you cut?

choices.label: Lower replication factor from 3 to 2 in the US serving DC
choices.resultBody: With RF 2, LOCAL_QUORUM needs both replicas: a single node restart makes its token ranges unavailable for reads and writes at that consistency, and availability drops toward 99.5%, breaking the 99.95% SLO.

choices.label: Shrink the analytics DC from 12 nodes to 5 (about 21% CPU)
choices.resultBody: The analytics ring serves no user reads, so shrinking it does not touch the serving path. Five nodes run near 21% CPU and still hold RF 3; the nightly job just takes 3 hours instead of 2. Saves about $11,000 a month.

choices.label: Drop the EU DC and serve European users from the US DC
choices.resultBody: Removing EU replicas saves the most, but every European read now crosses the Atlantic at about 90 ms RTT. EU read p99 rises from 9 ms to 105 ms, over the 50 ms SLO, and a US outage leaves EU with nothing.

hints: Serving DCs earn their keep; find the ring that does not serve users.
Compare RF and quorum size before dropping replicas.
Cut the DC whose CPU shows it is mostly idle.

incidents.title: Singapore follower refuses to serve prices
incidents.brief: ShopSphere's Singapore follower answers price reads only while its replication lag is under 1 s, otherwise it forwards to the US leader. 38% of 60,000 reads/s cross the ocean and p95 sits at 235 ms.
incidents.constraint: A price shown to a shopper may be at most 10 seconds old.
incidents.question: Set the follower's lag bound so most reads stay local without breaking the price rule.

choices.label: Serve follower reads while lag stays under a 5 to 10 s bound

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: A bounded-staleness read: fast and local, with a hard cap on how old the data can be.

choices.resultTitle: Local reads with a hard freshness cap
choices.resultBody: With an 8 s bound the follower serves 97.5% of reads itself at about 50 ms and forwards only the reads that arrive during a lag spike, so the leader drops from 36% to 22% CPU and p95 from 235 ms to 52 ms. Cost: a price can be up to 8 s old, and during a long replication stall every SG read pays the 180 ms trip.

choices.label: Always forward price reads to the US leader to keep them fresh
choices.resultTitle: Fresh prices, an ocean on every read
choices.resultBody: Every one of the 60,000 reads/s now crosses to the US, adding about 180 ms of round trip, so p95 stays near 240 ms and the leader's CPU climbs from 36% to 62%. Prices are always current, but the follower in Singapore sits idle and an undersea cable fault would take reads down.

choices.label: Serve every follower read locally, whatever the replication lag
choices.resultBody: Reads are local and p95 falls to 45 ms, but a weekly vacuum stall on the leader pushes follower lag to 40 s for 6 minutes. During those stalls about 0.9% of reads, roughly 540 a second, show prices older than the 10 s limit, and the first checkout mismatch becomes a support ticket.

nodes.sub: serving prices up to 40 s old

hints: There is no partition today: this is the latency half of PACELC, not the availability half.
A bound that is too tight sends most reads across the ocean; one that is too loose breaks the 10-second price rule.
Pick a lag bound close to the staleness the business accepts, but not above it.

knob.label: Follower lag bound
knob.question: Set the lag bound so most reads stay local and no price is older than 10 s.

low.title: Too tight, reads cross the ocean
low.body: Below 5 s the follower rejects normal replication lag, so between 4% and 100% of reads go to the US leader at up to 240 ms and the leader runs at 22% to 62% CPU.

high.title: Too loose, prices break the rule
high.body: Above 10 s the follower keeps serving through lag spikes, so 0.6% to 0.9% of reads, hundreds a second, show prices older than the 10-second limit.

good.title: Local reads, bounded staleness
good.body: At 5 to 10 s the follower serves 96% to 99% of reads locally at about 50 ms, forwards only during lag spikes, and no shopper sees a price older than 10 s.
